content: The following solvents are prohibited for use in aerosol formulations: benzene, 2-butoxyethanol (ethylene glycol monobutyl ether), 2-butoxyethyl acetate (ethylene glycol monobutyl ether acetate), carbon tetrachloride, chlorobenzene, chloroform, 1,2-dichloroethane (ethylene dichloride), 2-ethoxyethanol (ethylene glycol monoethyl ether), 2-ethoxyethyl acetate (ethylene glycol monoethyl ether acetate), n-hexane, 2-hexanone (methyl n-butyl ketone), 2-methoxyethanol (ethylene glycol monomethyl ether), 2-methoxyethyl acetate (ethylene glycol monomethyl ether acetate), tetrachloroethylene, and trichloroethylene. The Montreal Protocol and the EU directive regarding the phase-out of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) in aerosols are acknowledged. Hydrocarbon propellants are recommended for use in insecticide aerosols, provided that the aerosol producer adheres to international safety standards. The industry is encouraged to develop alternative and safer propellants and delivery systems. Analytical methods must comply with CIPAC or AOAC standards. If these methods are unpublished, full details and appropriate validation data must be submitted to the WHO by the proposer. To prepare an aerosol container for analysis, it should be dried externally, then either immersed in dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) for at least one hour or placed in a deep freezer (-18°C or below) overnight. The container should then be removed to a fume hood, and using a suitable shield, punctured near the top with a sharp implement to create a hole or holes large enough for the introduction and removal of extraction solvent. Allow the propellant to evaporate by letting the contents return to room temperature without additional warming. Using a suitable solvent (appropriate for the active ingredient and synergist), thoroughly rinse the contents of the dispenser into a volumetric flask and make up the volume with the solvent. If possible, use a solvent that does not remove paint or other external coatings. Using an appropriate analytical method, determine the mass of active ingredient and synergist in the rinsate. Dry the rinsed dispenser and re-weigh it to determine the mass of the formulation it contained. Use this value to express the content of active ingredient and synergist on a g/kg basis. If the identity of the synergist is considered confidential, the JMPS will evaluate the requirements for this clause on a case-by-case basis. Analytical methods must be peer-validated or comply with CIPAC or AOAC standards. Only relevant impurities should be included in the clause, and the title should reflect the name of the relevant impurity. The determination of pressure in finished aerosol packs is necessary to verify that the true pressure is compatible with the pack's pressure limitations and complies with applicable regulations. True pressure is defined as the relative pressure measured by an accurate manometer at a given temperature. The method is recommended for determining the true pressure of all filled aerosol packs. The apparatus required includes a source of reference gas (e.g., nitrogen) with a pressure-regulating control valve and a high-accuracy manometer, preferably cushioned by an oil bath and adapted to fit the aerosol container. The apparatus must be assembled to ensure minimal impact on the true pressure value and to prevent contamination of the manometer by the pressurized product. To measure the true pressure, ensure the aerosol dispenser is equilibrated to 30 ± 2°C. Fit the measuring apparatus with an appropriate adapter for the valve used. Regulate the reference gas pressure to a value slightly higher than the anticipated pressure of the dispenser. Apply the measuring apparatus to the valve, press lightly to open the valve, and read the true pressure on the manometer once the needle stabilizes. The accuracy of the measurement improves with larger aerosol dispenser sizes, minimal pressure differences between the reference gas and the dispenser's true pressure, and a small dead volume in the manometer (less than 2 mL). The test report must include results, test conditions, and any relevant working details not specified in the method, especially if they may have influenced the results. Frequent recalibration of the manometer is necessary, for example, using a manometric balance. The discharge rate of an aerosol dispenser is determined by measuring the quantity of material expelled through the valve over a specified time, typically 10 seconds. The temperature of the dispenser must be carefully controlled for reproducibility. The test is usually repeated three times to obtain three determinations. For products with vapor-phase tap valves, it is preferable to reduce the discharge interval to 5 seconds and the number of determinations to two to minimize composition variation during spraying. The discharge rate is calculated by dividing the weight difference by the discharge duration. Results may vary due to manufacturing tolerances, valve orifice diameter variations, or the effect of solvents on the gasket in freshly prepared dispensers. Long-lasting insecticidal nets (LNs) are nets or nettings made of monoor multi-filament fibers with one or more active ingredients incorporated into the filaments or coated onto their surface. Combination LNs may consist of different types of netting materials treated with different active ingredients. Specifications for combination LNs should be split into individual specifications for each netting material and one for the finished net. Manufacturers should minimize within-net heterogeneity of active ingredient distribution to ensure the relative standard deviation (RSD) for active ingredient content in five individual net pieces does not exceed 20%. Systematic variations in active ingredient content across or along netting could compromise efficacy, quality control, and safety. If systematic variation is suspected, special sampling procedures should be designed to test for its presence. The WHO defines acceptable LN performance as the retention of biological activity through 20 standard washes. However, there is no simple physicochemical measurement corresponding to this definition. Surface concentration of active ingredient is an important characteristic of LNs but is difficult to define and measure. It must be sufficient for efficacy but not excessive to avoid unacceptable user exposure or excessive losses through washing or weathering. Surface concentration may be used as a quality control criterion during production but is too variable for use thereafter. Control of mosquitoes (measured as mortality or knockdown) declines sharply within narrow ranges of surface concentration, with critical ranges differing between and within products. Consequently, highly accurate and precise analytical methods to measure surface concentrations after 20 washes are unnecessary, nor should they be used to develop limits for WHO specifications. WHO specifications should provide limits and methods indicating whether retention/release occurs but cannot guarantee acceptable efficacy before or after 20 standard washes.
